#10140. Falcon Perception

TL;DR — Falcon Perception is a 0.6B-parameter early-fusion Transformer for open-vocabulary grounding and segmentation from natural language prompts. The model processes image patches + text in one sequence using a hybrid attention mask, and produces variable numbers of instances with a small, structured token interface and lightweight output heads. On SA-Co, Falcon Perception reaches 68.0 Macro-F1 (vs. 62.3 for SAM 3) with the main remaining gap being presence calibration (MCC 0.64 vs. 0.82). We also introduce PBench, a diagnostic benchmark that breaks down performance by capability (attributes, OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, relations) and by dense long-context crowded scenes.

We also relase Falcon OCR, a 0.3B-parameter model which reaches a score of 80.3 and 88.6 on the olmOCR benchmark and OmniDocBench respectively, while having the highest throughput of any open source OCR model.

This post is a brief, practical write-up of what we built, why we built it this way, and what we learned along the way.

Many open-vocabulary perception systems are built as modular pipelines: a (often frozen) vision backbone extracts features, a separate fusion/decoder stage combines them with language, and additional components handle matching and post-processing. This family of designs works well in many settings, but it comes with trade-offs: it can be hard to scale cleanly, hard to attribute improvements to the right component, and easy to accumulate complexity as we add a new fix for each failure mode.

We asked a simpler question: can a single early-fusion Transformer backbone handle both perception and language modeling, if we choose the right attention pattern, output interface, and training signal?

In our experiments, the answer is largely yes. The rest of this post describes the main design choices and the evidence behind them.

A single autoregressive Transformer processes a unified sequence of image patches, text, and task tokens. The model predicts object properties in a fixed order: → → . Bounding box coordinates and sizes are decoded via specialized heads and re-injected as Fourier features. High-resolution segmentation masks are generated by a dot product between the token and upsampled image features.

At its core, Falcon Perception is a dense Transformer that processes image patches and text tokens in a shared parameter space from the first layer. Instead of a separate vision backbone followed by a late-fusion decoder, we keep a single backbone and rely on masking and a lightweight output interface to make the dense prediction problem tractable.

Images and text have different structure: pixels are 2D and benefit from bidirectional context, while the prediction interface is naturally sequential. We address this with a hybrid attention mask:

This allows the same backbone to behave like a bidirectional visual encoder on image tokens, while still supporting autoregressive prediction over task tokens.

Dense perception is not a fixed-size prediction problem: an image may contain zero instances or hundreds. Autoregressive generation gives a clean variable-length interface, but fully autoregressive dense generation (e.g., polygons or high-resolution masks token-by-token) quickly becomes expensive.

We use a small structured interface, Chain-of-Perception, which decomposes each instance into three steps:

This ordering is deliberate. Committing to geometry first reduces ambiguity (“which instance?”), and makes the mask prediction step closer to pixel refinement conditioned on the resolved object.

The backbone is shared, while decoding uses lightweight heads tailored to the output type:

Coordinate & Size Heads use Fourier feature encoding : mapping continuous coordinates through a random Gaussian projection into a high-dimensional sinusoidal space. This overcomes the spectral bias of neural networks, yielding more precise localization than discrete binning alone. Decoded coordinates are re-injected into the sequence as conditioning for subsequent tokens.

Segmentation Head computes a dot product between the token’s hidden state and content-aware upsampled image features. Because the token is produced after geometry and has access to early-fused visual context, we can avoid the separate mask-query machinery and Hungarian matching that often appears in decoder-based instance segmentation training.

Existing referring-expression benchmarks like RefCOCO are saturated — models routinely hit 90%+ — and they conflate what went wrong. Did the model fail because it can't read text? Can't understand spatial relationships? Can't handle a crowd?

We introduce PBench, a diagnostic benchmark that separates samples by the dominant capability required:

Each sample targets one dominant capability: OCR prompts avoid spatial qualifiers, and spatial prompts avoid in-image text disambiguators. This yields a capability profile rather than a single opaque score, and makes it easier to decide where to invest next (data, training curriculum, or post-training).

Rather than training from random weights (which in our ablations was unstable for segmentation), Falcon Perception initializes via multi-teacher distillation. Two strong vision teachers contribute complementary signals:

The distilled initialization achieves 74.25% zero-shot accuracy on ImageNet-1k and 85.11% linear-probe mIoU on Pascal VOC, providing a strong visual foundation before perception-specific training.

We build the training set through a multi-stage pipeline:

We maintain a strict 1:1 ratio of positive to negative samples. This makes presence calibration a first-class target: the model should reliably say “absent,” not only draw masks when confident.

Stage 1 — In-Context Listing (450 GT): The model learns to autoregressively list scene inventories — predicting text expressions and their locations. Full causal attention between queries enables learning of object co-occurrence ("fork, then knife, then plate"). This builds broad scene understanding.

Stage 2 — Task Alignment (225 GT): The attention mask is modified so queries can no longer see each other, simulating independent queries at inference time. Loss on text tokens is masked, focusing gradient signal entirely on presence classification and localization. This stage transitions from "scene understanding" to "answer this specific question."

Stage 3 — Long-Context Finetuning (10 GT): A short phase with the mask limit raised to 600 per expression and a minimal constant learning rate. This adapts the model for extreme crowd density without forgetting earlier capabilities.

Key design choices validated through ablations:

On the SA-Co open-vocabulary segmentation benchmark, Falcon Perception (0.6B parameters) achieves 68.0 Macro-F1, compared to 62.3 for SAM 3, with large gains on attribute-heavy (+8.2), food & drink (+12.2), and sports equipment (+4.0) splits. At the same time, Falcon Perception lags SAM 3 on presence calibration (MCC: 0.64 vs 0.82), which is the clearest remaining improvement axis.

Here's an example output — the prompt "Falcon" produces precise instance masks:

Falcon Perception also performs well for reffering expressions, able to correctly segment the burger with a black bun in each frame of the video:

This is where the early-fusion design shows the largest differences:

On simple objects, the gap is modest. As prompts become more compositional—requiring OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, or relational binding—the gap widens.

In our PBench Dense split, Falcon Perception (0.6B) substantially outperforms generalist VLM baselines (e.g., 72.6 vs 8.9 for Qwen3-VL-30B in our evaluation setup), and matches or exceeds the 8B model on spatial and relational tiers.

As prompts grow more compositional — requiring OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, relational binding, or scaling to hundreds of instances — the early-fusion advantage becomes visually clear:

"168 wine bottles": Falcon Perception identifies the bottles labeled "168", while SAM 3 highlights every bottle. "Honolulu direction sign": Falcon reads the text to find the right sign.

"Lower meat skewer on left grill," "black car to the right of red car at bottom," "Belgian flag on the left" — Falcon Perception resolves the correct instance from spatial constraints. SAM 3 predicts false positives for multiple candidates.

"Pastry next to brown round bread," "person using phone," "person holding helmet in hand" — Falcon Perception identifies the interacting instance. SAM 3 highlights all instances of the object class, ignoring the relational constraint.

"Snow goose," "pigeon," "colorful canned drinks" — Falcon Perception autoregressively segments hundreds of instances. SAM 3's fixed-size decoder runs out of query tokens beyond ~200 instances.

Modern OCR has moved well beyond extracting text from clean scans. Today's systems must handle multi-column layouts, mathematical formulas, tables, charts, and multilingual content — all in one pass. Most competitive OCR VLMs tackle this with a familiar recipe: a vision encoder feeding a separate text decoder, plus task-specific glue. These systems work, but they tend to be large (1B–3B+ parameters).

We took a different path: reuse the same early-fusion dense Transformer from Falcon Perception, but train a smaller 0.3B-parameter variant from scratch specifically for OCR. The result is Falcon OCR — a single backbone that processes image patches and text tokens in a shared parameter space with the same hybrid attention mask (bidirectional for image tokens, causal for text tokens), and switches tasks through prompts rather than additional modules.

We trained from scratch (no multi-teacher distillation) because the visual features OCR needs — fine-grained glyph recognition, stroke-level discrimination — differ substantially from the object-level features useful for segmentation. Starting fresh lets the backbone develop text-optimized representations from the ground up.

We train on a curated English-language mixture spanning three core tasks: general document text parsing (digital PDFs, old scans, typewritten documents), mathematical and scientific formula recognition, and table structure recognition. The mixture also includes handwriting, real-world scene text, and synthetic samples generated from rendered LaTeX and HTML sources. The training objective is pure next-token prediction on structured text outputs.

Training proceeds in two phases: a long pre-training phase at constant learning rate where the model learns core OCR capabilities across all element types, followed by a short cosine-decay finetuning phase where the learning rate is annealed to near zero.

We evaluate on olmOCR (binary correctness checks across diverse inputs) and OmniDocBench (continuous metrics over full-page parses). All comparison models are significantly larger and/or use proprietary infrastructure. At 80.3% on olmOCR with only 0.3B parameters, Falcon OCR is within 1.7 points of the top system and leads all models on Multi-Column (87.1%) and Tables (90.3%). On OmniDocBench it scores 88.64 overall, ahead of DeepSeek OCR v2, GPT 5.2, and Mistral OCR 3.

At 0.3B parameters, Falcon OCR is roughly 3x smaller than 0.9B-class OCR VLMs, which translates directly into higher serving throughput. Measured on a single A100-80GB with vLLM at high concurrency:

The compact footprint and vLLM integration (continuous batching, PagedAttention, optimized CUDA kernels) make it practical for large-scale document digitization where millions of pages need processing.

More broadly, these results suggest that the early-fusion single-stack Transformer is a viable alternative to the "vision encoder plus text decoder" recipe for OCR. One backbone, shared parameter space, one decoding interface, and better data and training signals rather than increasingly complex pipelines. We hope this encourages more work in this direction.

Falcon OCR processes images captured under challenging real-world conditions with varying lighting, diverse text semantics (mathematical formulae, structured tables, handwritten notes), and complex document layouts, to produce structured text output.

Falcon OCR extracts text from handwritten documents and real-world photographs with variable lighting, orientation, and content complexity.

Falcon OCR accurately reproduces cell entries and structural layout from tables of varying formats and complexity.

Falcon OCR correctly transcribes mathematical expressions ranging from simple equations to multi-line derivations with nested operators.

Falcon OCR preserves reading order and structural fidelity when extracting text from documents with multi-column layouts, figures, and footnotes.

The release includes an inference stack built on PyTorch’s FlexAttention, which makes it practical to express the custom attention patterns and efficiently serve packed variable-length sequences.

In our setup on an H100, typical latencies are on the order of ~100ms prefill, ~200ms upsampling (0ms if cached), and ~50ms decode for a handful of instances. (These numbers depend on resolution, sequence length, and the number of predicted instances.)

For the Falcon-OCR model, we also provide a vLLM docker server for fast deployment and MLX integration for Apple-Silicon

Please check out the github repo for details.

Falcon Perception is intentionally minimal: one backbone, one objective family, and small heads only where outputs are continuous and dense. The working assumption is that most gains should come from data, compute, and training signals, rather than continually expanding the pipeline with specialized modules.

The architecture doesn't block any obvious scaling path: add more images and harder prompts for better grounding, mix in text-only data for better language, increase context length for denser scenes. It's still just one sequence model.

Falcon Perception is developed by the Falcon Vision Team at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII), Abu Dhabi, UAE.

If you use Falcon-Perception, please cite

#10139. Best Ecommerce Platforms for Developers: Six Options and the Layers Each Leaves You

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

Shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that plan. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide shows how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

WooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

BigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the company says you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

#10138. Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec

For most of the last decade, an API call looked like a transaction. A client sent a request, waited, and got a complete response back in one piece. That model is exactly what most API management tooling — including API Gateway — was built to handle, and it still describes a huge amount of production traffic.

But that no longer describes all traffic types. A model generating a response emits tokens as it produces them, not in one batch at the end. An agent working through a multi-step task reports progress as it goes. A dashboard, a collaborative editor, a live inference endpoint — these all need a connection that stays open and carries data in both directions.

Until now, developers building those experiences in API Gateway had to make an uncomfortable choice: put API Gateway in front of their APIs and give up streaming, or route streaming endpoints around the gateway and give up the authentication, API key enforcement, and observability that made the gateway essential in the first place. Teams ended up with a split estate — governed APIs on one path, ungoverned streaming traffic on another.

We're announcing that streaming support in API Gateway is available in Public Preview. Your streaming endpoints can now sit behind the same gateway, with the same policies, as everything else you serve.

For AI applications, streaming also strengthens API Gateway's connection to Gemini platform. A gateway that uses model routing now streams responses from Gemini, Claude and OpenAI gpt-oss models in model garden in Gemini platform as they're generated, and streaming backends you host anywhere else work the same way. Alongside Apigee and Agent Gateway in Gemini platform, API Gateway is the lightweight entry point to Google Cloud's AI gateway capabilities.

API Gateway now supports the full range of streaming patterns modern APIs rely on:

Streams can stay open for up to one hour. As with any long-lived connection, clients should implement reconnection logic so that a session survives the end of a stream — a well-behaved WebSocket or SSE client should be doing this anyway.

This is the part we are most pleased with: there is nothing new to learn.

Streaming is not a different product, a different resource type, or a different way of describing your API. There are no new extensions to add, no streaming-specific annotations, no separate spec for streaming operations. The same document that describes your existing API describes your streaming API.

Everything you already rely on continues to work exactly as before:

During Public Preview, you opt-in when creating the gateway:

That single flag is the entire difference. At GA, it is planned that streaming will simply be how API Gateway behaves, with no opt-in required and, as during Preview, no changes to your API config.

Alongside streaming, gateways get a deterministic default hostname:

Previously the default gateway.dev hostname included a generated hash, which meant you could not know your gateway's URL until after you had created it. That is a small thing that causes a lot of friction: you can't write the endpoint into a client config, a Terraform module, a CI pipeline, a firewall allowlist, or a partner integration doc until the resource exists — and if you tear the environment down and rebuild it, the URL changes underneath you.

Now the hostname is a pure function of values you already chose. You can generate it, template it, document it, and commit it to source control before the gateway exists, and you get the same URL every time you rebuild the same gateway in the same project and region. For anyone managing environments as code, or promoting a configuration from dev to staging to prod, this removes an entire category of bootstrapping problem.

Streaming isn't a niche feature for AI applications — it's the expected interaction pattern.

Users expect to see a model's response appear as it's generated, not after a thirty-second pause. Agents need to report intermediate steps. Tool-calling protocols and remote MCP servers depend on long-lived, incrementally-delivered connections. An API management layer that can't stream severely limits the user experience of AI applications.

With streaming, API Gateway becomes a viable front door for that agentic traffic — and the value of a front door is exactly the same as it's always been, only more urgent. AI endpoints are expensive, they consume quota, they need per-consumer authentication and rate limiting, and they need to be observable. These are the governance problems that an AI gateway is intended to solve. The alternative — every team standing up its own proxy in front of its own model endpoint — is how organizations end up unable to answer basic questions about who is calling what.

Model routing in API Gateway lets you expose a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint and dispatch requests to Gemini, Claude, or OpenAI gpt-oss models based on the model field in the request payload. Model routing plus streaming means clients get a familiar, standards-based streaming interface, while you retain centralized control over which models are reachable, by whom, and under what policy.

Streaming, model routing and MCP support are all features within API Gateway that provide a lightweight on-ramp to AI gateway capabilities within Google Cloud. These AI gateway capabilities allow teams to monitor, secure and control agentic traffic of tools, models and agents in their ecosystem, and they're delivered as a composable suite so you can choose the right gateway for each use case. For more expansive AI policies and full lifecycle management, use Apigee. To manage and secure agent connectivity, use Agent Gateway in Gemini platform. You can also combine these gateways: API Gateway or Apigee can sit in front of your agents and APIs, or behind Agent Gateway so your agents can reach models, tools, and MCP servers. For example, you can route your agent's egress through Agent Gateway for strict security governance, and then pass the request to API Gateway to handle model routing.

A few things to plan around while the feature is in Preview:

If you're already using API Gateway, the fastest way to see this working is to point a new streaming-enabled gateway at an existing backend that emits SSE and watch the events arrive incrementally. No spec changes needed.

#10137. Welcome Gemma 4: Frontier multimodal intelligence on device

The Gemma 4 family of multimodal models by Google DeepMind is out on Hugging Face, with support for your favorite agents, inference engines, and fine-tuning libraries 🤗

These models are the real deal: truly open with Apache 2 licenses, high quality with pareto frontier arena scores, multimodal including audio, and sizes you can use everywhere including on-device. Gemma 4 builds on advances from previous families and makes them click together. In our tests with pre-release checkpoints we have been impressed by their capabilities, to the extent that we struggled to find good fine-tuning examples because they are so good out of the box.

We collaborated with Google and the community to make them available everywhere: transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, WebGPU, Rust; you name it. This blog post will show you how to build with your favorite tools so let us know what you think!

Similar to Gemma-3n, Gemma 4 supports image, text, and audio inputs, and generates text responses. The text decoder is based on the Gemma model with support for long context windows. The image encoder is similar to the one from Gemma 3 but with two crucial improvements: variable aspect ratios, and configurable number of image token inputs to find your sweet spot between speed, memory, and quality. All models support images (or video) and text inputs, while the small variants (E2B, E4B) and the 12B Unified model support audio as well.

Gemma 4 comes in five sizes, all base and instruction fine-tuned:

Gemma 4 leverages several architecture components used in previous Gemma versions and other open models, and leaves out complex or inconclusive features such as Altup. The combination is a mix designed to be highly compatible across libraries and devices, that can efficiently support long context and agentic use cases, whilst being ideal for quantization.

As shown in the benchmarks above, this feature mix (combined with the training data and recipe) enables the 31B dense model to achieve an estimated LMArena score (text only) of 1452, while the 26B MoE reaches 1441 with just 4B active parameters 🤯. As we'll see, multimodal operation is comparatively as good as text generation, at least in informal and subjective tests.

These are the main architecture characteristics in Gemma 4:

One of the most distinctive features in smaller Gemma 4 models is Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which was introduced previously in Gemma-3n. In a standard transformer, each token gets a single embedding vector at input, and the same initial representation is what the residual stream builds on across all layers, forcing the embedding to frontload everything the model might need. PLE adds a parallel, lower-dimensional conditioning pathway alongside the main residual stream. For each token, it produces a small dedicated vector for every layer by combining two signals: a token-identity component (from an embedding lookup) and a context-aware component (from a learned projection of the main embeddings). Each decoder layer then uses its corresponding vector to modulate the hidden states via a lightweight residual block after attention and feed-forward. This gives each layer its own channel to receive token-specific information only when it becomes relevant, rather than requiring everything to be packed into a single upfront embedding. Because the PLE dimension is much smaller than the main hidden size, this adds meaningful per-layer specialization at modest parameter cost. For multimodal inputs (images, audio, video), PLE is computed before soft tokens are merged into the embedding sequence — since PLE relies on token IDs that are lost once multimodal features replace the placeholders. Multimodal positions use the pad token ID, effectively receiving neutral per-layer signals.

The shared KV cache is an efficiency optimization that reduces both compute and memory during inference. The last num_kv_shared_layers layers of the model don't compute their own key and value projections. Instead, they reuse the K and V tensors from the last non-shared layer of the same attention type (sliding or full).

In practice, this has a minimal impact on quality while being much more efficient (in terms of both memory and compute) for long context generation and on-device use.

The Gemma 4 12B Unified model has no separate vision or audio encoder. Instead, raw image patches and audio waveforms are projected directly into the LLM's embedding space through lightweight linear layers, and all modalities flow into a single decoder-only transformer. This reduces multimodal latency and allows the whole model to be fine-tuned in one pass. The checkpoint size makes it deployment-friendly on consumer hardware.

We saw in our tests that Gemma 4 supports comprehensive multimodal capabilities out of the box. We don't know what was the training mix, but we had success using it for tasks such as OCR, speech-to-text, object detection, or pointing. It also supports text-only and multimodal function calling, reasoning, code completion and correction.

Here, we show a few inference examples across different model sizes. You can run them conveniently with this notebook. We encourage you to try the demos and share them below this blog!

mistral.rs is a Rust-native inference engine with day-0 Gemma 4 support across all modalities (text, image, video, audio) and builtin tool-calling and agentic functionality. Install mistral.rs:

Google has released Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) drafters for the Gemma 4 family: small assistant models that accelerate inference via speculative decoding. The drafter proposes several future tokens at once, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass. You get the same outputs as the target model, just faster — no quality loss, no changes to reasoning behaviour. Reported end-to-end speedups go up to ~3x depending on hardware, batch size, and workload.

Assistants are available for all four Gemma 4 sizes (E2B, E4B, 26B A4B, 31B). They share the KV cache with the target model to avoid recomputing context, and the smaller edge variants additionally use an embedder clustering trick to keep memory and compute low on-device.

Find the checkpoints in the Gemma 4 collection and the mlx-community collection.

Alongside the autoregressive Gemma 4 family, Google DeepMind is releasing DiffusionGemma, a multimodal model that generates text using discrete diffusion instead of token-by-token autoregression. It's built on the same 26B A4B Mixture-of-Experts foundation (25.2B total / 3.8B active parameters, 8 active experts out of 128 plus 1 shared), takes text and image inputs, generates text, and supports up to 256K context — all under the same Apache 2.0 license.

Where a standard causal LM emits one token at a time, DiffusionGemma denoises whole blocks of tokens in parallel. The architecture is encoder-decoder: an autoregressive encoder prefills the prompt and builds the KV cache, while a decoder applies bidirectional attention over a "canvas" of 256 tokens. During multi-canvas sampling, the model iteratively denoises a full canvas with a diffusion sampler; once a canvas is finalized it's encoded and appended to the KV cache, then the next canvas begins. This block-autoregressive approach increases generation speed.

The headline benefit is throughput: parallel denoising generates roughly 15–20 tokens per forward pass, reaching per-user generation speeds exceeding 1100 tokens/second at low batch sizes (H100, FP8). Inference compute is adaptive too — simpler prompts and structured tasks like code need fewer denoising steps, so tokens-per-second scales with task complexity. It keeps the broader Gemma 4 toolkit: thinking mode, function calling, long context, native system prompts, and image understanding (OCR, document parsing, object detection, pointing) at variable aspect ratios and resolutions.

Benchmarks show an expected trade-off between speed and evaluation metrics — DiffusionGemma trails the autoregressive 26B A4B on most tasks (e.g. MMLU Pro 77.6% vs 82.6%, AIME 2026 69.1% vs 88.3%, GPQA Diamond 73.2% vs 82.3%) in exchange for its large speed advantage, while edging ahead on a few (HLE no tools 11.0% vs 8.7%).

Getting started looks just like the rest of Gemma 4, via the dedicated diffusion class:

For best results, Google recommends the Entropy-Bounded (EB) sampler with adaptive stopping (up to 48 denoising steps, a temperature schedule decaying from 0.8 → 0.4, and an entropy bound of 0.1 for token selection). As with Gemma 4, place image content before text in your prompt, and toggle reasoning with the <|think|> control token.

Gemma 4 models are ideal for fine-tuning in your favorite tools and platforms and at any budget.

Gemma 4 is fully supported for fine-tuning with TRL. To celebrate, TRL has been upgraded with support for multimodal tool responses when interacting with environments, meaning models can now receive images back from tools during training, not just text.

To showcase this, we've built an example training script where Gemma 4 learns to drive in the CARLA simulator. The model sees the road through a camera, decides what to do and learns from the outcome. After training, it consistently changes lanes to avoid pedestrians. The same approach works for any task where a model needs to see and act: robotics, web browsing, or other interactive environments.

Additionally, we have prepared an example on how to fine-tune Gemma 4 with TRL on Vertex AI using SFT, to showcase how to extend the function calling capabilities, whilst freezing both the vision and audio towers. The examples include how to build a custom Docker container with latest Transformers, TRL, etc. with CUDA support on Google Cloud, and how to run it via Vertex AI Serverless Training Jobs.

You can find the complete example in the "Hugging Face on Google Cloud" docs at https://hf.co/docs/google-cloud/examples/vertex-ai-notebooks-fine-tune-gemma-4.

one gap worth flagging for anyone building on Gemma 4's function calling for real-world deployments: when the model generates a function call, there's currently no verifiable record that a human principal authorized that specific action. a compromised system prompt or injected instruction produces a call that's indistinguishable from legitimate delegation at the tool interface.

i opened a PR on the gemma-cookbook repo today that adds a drop-in HDP middleware layer to address this, sits between Gemma 4's function call output and tool execution, verifies Ed25519-signed delegation tokens, classifies actions by irreversibility (Class 0–3), and blocks unauthorized calls pre-execution.

for edge/robotics deployments (E2B on Jetson Nano / Raspberry Pi directing actuators), there's a companion HDP-P extension covering the physical layer.

#10136. Your SSL certificates can now last 200 days at most: The real risk isn’t renewal

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan. Following the latest update from the CA/Browser Forum, the maximum lifetime of a certificate has fallen from 398 days to 200, and it will drop to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Renewal is no longer an annual chore. It’s an ongoing task that only stays manageable with automation.

So what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes? For many setups, very little will change. For others, one missed renewal can mean an outage. This article explains what’s changing and what to do if you’re in the second group.

Today, an SSL certificate is valid for 200 days at most. The limit applies when a certificate is issued, so the ones you already hold keep their original expiration date.

Where you feel it depends on how your certificates renew. Sites on managed hosting platforms or behind a content delivery network (CDN) usually renew automatically already, often every 90 days, so the new limit changes little. The pressure lands on setups where someone buys a certificate once a year and installs it by hand. At 47 days, that becomes about 12 renewals a year.

A certificate is a promise from a certificate authority that a key really belongs to a domain, and that promise gets less reliable the longer it runs. If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, it stays usable until it expires. Cutting the lifetime shrinks that window, so a problem that once lingered for over a year is now fixed in weeks.

Shorter lifetimes also make revocation, the process for canceling a bad certificate, far less critical. Revocation has never worked perfectly, but a certificate that expires within weeks matters much less if a cancellation doesn’t reach every browser.

Another reason is about people. A task done once a year is easy to forget and hard to check from outside. Browser makers have pushed for years to move the industry onto automatic renewal, on the logic that a process that runs every few weeks gets tested constantly. If it breaks, you notice quickly instead of discovering it on the day the certificate expires.

For most people, the first effect is simply more work. A certificate that once needed attention every year will soon need it every few weeks. Plus, each renewal is a small chance for something to go wrong. Multiply that by dozens of sites, mail servers, and devices, and the chance of one slipping through grows quickly.

The safety nets are also thinner. If you relied on the renewal emails, nothing is watching your certificates now. Additionally, with a shorter life, there’s less time between this should have renewed and this has expired.

An expired certificate doesn’t make a site slow or dated. It makes it unreachable for most visitors. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all show a full-page warning that the connection isn’t private, and most people leave instead of clicking through. If the site uses HSTS, a setting that tells browsers to connect only over secure links, there is often no way to click through at all, and visitors are blocked outright until the certificate is fixed.

The damage doesn’t stop at the home page. Checkouts, contact forms, and logins that depend on the secure connection fail along with it, often without an error message that points at the real cause. Other systems break, too, because apps and integrations that call your site over a secure link refuse to connect to an expired certificate.

Nothing about your site has to change for any of this to happen. A date passes, and a site that worked on Friday is down on Monday. In a 47-day lifetime, that date comes around about every six weeks.

Automatic renewal tools do the heavy lifting well. The failures happen around them:

Look at the five failures above and you’ll see what they share. Each one happens quietly. The renewal job ran, or looked like it did, and nobody checked what the server was actually serving afterwards. Automation can tell you it tried. It can’t tell you the result reached your visitors.

What closes that gap is a check that never relies on your server’s own account of events. Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring does exactly that. It reads the certificate installed on your web server from the cloud, the way a visitor’s browser would, and alerts you before it expires, using thresholds you choose. If a renewal fails quietly, you hear about it from the monitor and not from a customer.

For each certificate, it records the issuing authority, the owner, the issue date, the expiration date, and the days remaining, including on servers that host several certificates behind one address. That last number matters more as lifespans shrink. When a certificate lasts 47 days, the days left is the figure that tells you a renewal is overdue, and you can set your warning against it using the quarter-of-the-lifetime rule covered next.

Once a monitor is watching your certificates, the next question is when it should speak up.

Most expiration alerts are set to a fixed number of days: warn at 30 days left and escalate at seven. That works for a certificate that lasts a year and renews with a month to spare. It breaks when the whole certificate lasts for a limited number of days.

Here’s why: a healthy certificate renews with about a third of its life still left. If your alert appears earlier than that, it goes off on certificates that are doing nothing wrong, and soon everyone ignores it. As lifespans shrink, a fixed 30-day alert will start doing exactly that.

The fix is to set the alerts based on lateness, not on how close the expiry date is. Warn when a quarter of the lifetime is left, since a renewal is overdue by then, and escalate when a tenth is left. Because these are shares of the lifetime, they keep working, however short lifespans get.

The next cut lands on March 15, 2027, so a few checks now will save you from scrambling later:

Shorter lifespans won’t break your site, but a missed renewal will, so fix the quiet failures now while a mistake still costs an afternoon to fix, not a Monday morning outage affecting lots of customers.

If you’d like a second pair of eyes on your certificates, you can start a 30-day free trial of Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring.

#10135. Safetensors is Joining the PyTorch Foundation

Today, we're announcing that Safetensors has joined the PyTorch Foundation as a foundation-hosted project under the Linux Foundation, alongside DeepSpeed, Helion, Ray, vLLM, and PyTorch itself.

Safetensors started as a Hugging Face project born out of a concrete need: a way to store and share model weights that couldn't execute arbitrary code. The pickle-based formats that dominated the ecosystem at the time meant that there was a very real risk you’d be running malicious code. While this was an acceptable risk when ML was still budding, it would become unacceptable as open model sharing became central to how the ML community works.

The format we built is intentionally simple: a JSON header with a hard limit of 100MB, describing tensor metadata, followed by raw tensor data. Zero-copy loading that maps tensors directly from disk. Lazy loading so you can read individual weights without deserializing an entire checkpoint.

What we didn't fully anticipate was how broadly it would be adopted. Today, Safetensors is the default format for model distribution across the Hugging Face Hub and others, used by tens of thousands of models across all modalities in ML. It has become the preferred way for the open source ML community to share models.

We want Safetensors to truly belong to the community. The project has always been open source, but code contributions are just one part of its evolution. By bringing more companies and contributors into the governance of the project, we make sure that progress reflects the breadth of the community building on top of it. Joining the PyTorch Foundation means Safetensors now has a vendor-neutral home. The trademark, the repository, and the governance of the project sit with the Linux Foundation rather than any single company. Hugging Face's two core maintainers, Luc and Daniel, remain on the Technical Steering Committee and continue to lead the project day-to-day, but Safetensors now formally belongs to the community that depends on it.

We believe safety is best guaranteed when every contributor can build on what already exists; a principle now embedded in the project's governance itself.

For the vast majority of users, nothing changes. The format is the same, the APIs are the same, the Hub integration is the same: no breaking changes. Models stored in Safetensors format today will continue to work exactly as they do now.

For contributors, the path to becoming a maintainer is now formally documented and open to anyone in the community. The project's governance lives in GOVERNANCE.md and MAINTAINERS.md in the repository. For organizations building on top of Safetensors, neutral governance under the Linux Foundation provides a stable, long-term foundation, entirely community-driven.

Safetensors is a well-established project, adopted by the ecosystem at large, but we're still convinced we're at the very beginning of the project.

We're working with the PyTorch team so that Safetensors may be used within PyTorch core as a serialization system for torch models.

The coming months will see significant growth, and we couldn't think of a better home for that next chapter than the PyTorch Foundation. The roadmap ahead includes device-aware loading and saving, so tensors can load directly onto CUDA, ROCm, and other accelerators without unnecessary CPU staging.

We're also building first-class APIs for Tensor Parallel and Pipeline Parallel loading, so each rank or pipeline stage loads only the weights it needs. And as the ecosystem's quantization landscape continues to evolve, we'll be formalizing support for FP8, block-quantized formats like GPTQ and AWQ, and sub-byte integer types.

These are problems the whole ecosystem has a stake in solving, and being inside the PyTorch Foundation means we can work on them in collaboration with the other hosted projects rather than in parallel.

Safetensors is open source and contributions are welcome at every level, from bug reports and documentation to new features and participation in governance.

If you're a developer, researcher, or organization that builds on Safetensors and want to be more involved in shaping its direction, open an issue, start a discussion, or reach out to the maintainers directly. The project has always belonged to the community that uses it. The governance now reflects that too.

Will there be a concerted effort now to get newer (and older) LLM models to adopt the more secure safetensors format rather than allowing AI developers to continue with pickle files as they did in the past? And what would some of the objections be, if any, for a developer to not transition to safetensors format?

#10134. Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v5.4 update, you can now encode and compare texts, images, audio, and videos using the same familiar API. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use these new multimodal capabilities for both embedding and reranking.

Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs. This opens up use cases like visual document retrieval, cross-modal search, and multimodal RAG pipelines.

If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

Traditional embedding models convert text into fixed-size vectors. Multimodal embedding models extend this by mapping inputs from different modalities (text, images, audio, or video) into a shared embedding space. This means you can compare a text query against image documents (or vice versa) using the same similarity functions you're already familiar with.

Similarly, traditional reranker (Cross Encoder) models compute relevance scores between pairs of texts. Multimodal rerankers can score pairs where one or both elements are images, combined text-image documents, or other modalities.

For example, you can compare a text query against image documents, find video clips matching a description, or build RAG pipelines that work across modalities.

Multimodal models require some extra dependencies. Install the extras for the modalities you need (see Installation for more details):

VLM-based models like Qwen3-VL-2B require a GPU with at least ~8 GB of VRAM. For the 8B variants, expect ~20 GB. If you don't have a local GPU, consider using a cloud GPU service or Google Colab. On CPU, these models will be extremely slow; text-only or CLIP models are better suited for CPU inference.

Loading a multimodal embedding model works exactly like loading a text-only model:

Some models might require a revision argument for now if the integration pull requests for the model is still pending. Once they're merged, you'll be able to load them without specifying a revision, like above.

The model automatically detects which modalities it supports, so there's nothing extra to configure. See Processor and Model kwargs if you want to control things like image resolution or model precision.

With a multimodal model loaded, model.encode() accepts images alongside text. Images can be provided as URLs, local file paths, or PIL Image objects (see Supported Input Types for all accepted formats):

You can compute similarities between text embeddings and image embeddings, since the model maps both into the same space:

As expected, "A green car parked in front of a yellow building" is most similar to the car image (0.51), and "A bee on a pink flower" is most similar to the bee image (0.67). The hard negatives ("A red car driving on a highway", "A wasp on a wooden table") correctly receive lower scores.

You might notice that even the best matching scores (0.51, 0.67) aren't very close to 1.0. This is due to the modality gap: embeddings from different modalities tend to cluster in separate regions of the space. Cross-modal similarities are typically lower than within-modal ones (e.g., text-to-text), but the relative ordering is preserved, so retrieval still works well.

For retrieval tasks, encode_query() and encode_document() are the recommended methods. Many retrieval models prepend different instruction prompts depending on whether the input is a query or a document, similar to how chat models might apply different system prompts depending on the goal. Model authors can specify their prompts in the model config, and encode_query() / encode_document() automatically load and apply the correct one:

Under the hood, both are thin wrappers around encode(), they just handle prompt selection for you. Here's what cross-modal retrieval looks like:

These methods accept the same input types as encode() (images, URLs, multimodal dicts, etc.) and pass through the same parameters. For models without specialized query/document prompts, they behave identically to encode().

Multimodal reranker (CrossEncoder) models score the relevance between pairs of inputs, where each element can be text, an image, audio, video, or a combination. They tend to outperform embedding models in terms of quality, but are slower since they process each pair individually. The currently available pretrained multimodal rerankers focus on text and image inputs, but the architecture supports any modality that the underlying model can handle.

The rank() method scores and ranks a list of documents against a query, supporting mixed modalities:

The reranker correctly identifies the car image (document 0) as the most relevant result, followed by the combined text+image document about a car in a European city (document 3). The bee image (document 1) scores lowest. Keep in mind that the modality gap can influence absolute scores: text-image pair scores may occupy a different range than text-text or image-image pair scores.

You can also check which modalities a reranker supports using modalities and supports(), just like with embedding models:

You can also use predict() to get raw relevance scores for specific pairs of inputs:

A common pattern is to use an embedding model for fast initial retrieval, then refine the top results with a reranker:

Since the corpus embeddings are pre-computed, the initial retrieval is fast even over millions of documents. The reranker then provides more accurate scoring over the smaller candidate set.

Multimodal models accept a variety of input formats. Here's a summary of what you can pass to model.encode():

You can check which modalities a model supports using the modalities property and supports() method:

The "message" modality indicates that the model accepts chat-style message inputs with interleaved content. In practice, you rarely need to use this directly. When you pass strings, URLs, or multimodal dicts, the model converts them to the appropriate message format internally. Sentence Transformers supports two message formats:

The format is auto-detected from the model's chat template.

Since all inputs get converted into the same message format internally, you can mix input types in a single encode() call:

If a model doesn't follow either format and you need full control, you can pass raw message dicts with role and content keys directly:

This bypasses the automatic format conversion and passes the messages directly to the processor's apply_chat_template().

You may want to control image resolution bounds or model precision. Use processor_kwargs and model_kwargs when loading the model:

See the SentenceTransformer API Reference documentation for more details on these kwargs.

In Sentence Transformers v5.4, tokenizer_kwargs has been renamed to processor_kwargs to reflect that multimodal models use processors rather than just tokenizers. The old name is still accepted but deprecated.

Here are the multimodal models supported in v5.4, also available in the v5.4 integrations collection:

The older CLIP models continue to be supported:

These simple CLIP models still work well on lower-resource hardware.

To learn how to finetune these multimodal models on your own data, see the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

The training companion to this post and adjacent Sentence Transformers guides:

#10133. Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Picture this. A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later. Congratulations, you now have a customer's name, phone number and card details sitting in a plain text log file that half the engineering team can open.

This happens more often than people admit. Logging AI calls is genuinely useful, but prompts and responses are some of the most personal text your application ever touches. Here's how to keep the usefulness and drop the risk.

A regular web request is easy to log: URL, status code, time taken. AI calls are messier.

The output changes from run to run. If a user says "your bot gave me a wrong answer yesterday", the only proof of what happened is what you sent and what came back at that moment. You can't just replay it and expect the same result.

Prompts are also built, not typed. The final text is usually a template, a few retrieved document chunks, some chat history and the user's message stitched together. When something looks off, the bug could be in any of those pieces, and only the assembled prompt shows you which one.

Then there's cost. You pay by the token, so without per-call records you can't say which feature is burning money. And quality drifts over time as models get upgraded and templates get edited. Old logs are your only baseline.

So yes, you need these logs. The real question is what goes into them.

Before writing any masking code, agree on what counts as sensitive. In most business apps that means:

Names, emails, phone numbers and home addresses

Card numbers, bank details and government ID numbers

Health, legal or job-related details people mention in free text

Internal material like contract wording, pricing rules or source code

The first three groups follow patterns, so they're easy to catch. The last two don't, and that's where most teams get caught out. Keep that in mind, because it shapes the design below.

The safest sensitive value is the one that never reaches the log. So split what you record into two buckets.

The first is metadata: a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. None of this is personal, and it answers most day-to-day questions.

The second is content, meaning the actual prompt and response text. You only need this when you're investigating quality, and even then you rarely need all of it. A sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call.

Here's a mistake that's easy to make: letting the log appender clean things up afterwards. By then the raw text may already be in a buffer, an async queue or a crash dump. Mask first, then log.

The cleanest way is one small component that every AI log call has to pass through:

public interface PiiMasker {     String mask(String input); }

Nothing else is allowed to write raw prompts. One chokepoint is much easier to review and test than masking sprinkled across fifty classes.

For structured data like emails, cards and tokens, regular expressions do the job well:

public class RegexPiiMasker implements PiiMasker {     private static final Map RULES = new LinkedHashMap<>();     static {         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9.%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"), "[EMAIL]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?\d{10}\b"), "[PHONE]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("(?i)bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9.~+/=-]+"), "Bearer [TOKEN]");     }     @Override     public String mask(String input) {         if (input == null || input.isBlank()) return input;         String result = input;         for (var rule : RULES.entrySet()) {             result = rule.getKey().matcher(result).replaceAll(rule.getValue());         }         return result;     } }

A few small choices matter here. The patterns are compiled once, not on every call. The order is fixed, because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. And the replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable, so whoever debugs it later can still follow what the user was asking.

Regex won't catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence. For those you have a few options, and they work best together.

You can run a named-entity recognition model that tags people, places and organisations, then mask anything above a confidence threshold. You can do exact replacement of values you already know, such as the customer's name from the current session. Or, best of all, you can mask at the field level while building the prompt. If your code knows that customer.getEmail() is going into the template, swap in a placeholder right there instead of trying to spot it afterwards. Knowing beats guessing every time.

Plain redaction can remove too much. If the same email shows up five times in a conversation, five identical [EMAIL] tags hide the fact that it was one person.

The fix is consistent pseudonyms. Turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. You can still follow the thread, but nobody can read the original from the log. Use an HMAC with a secret from your secrets manager. A plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes, because there just aren't that many phone numbers.

One warning: if you also store a lookup table to reverse the tokens, that table is now sensitive data too. Most teams are better off with one-way tokens.

Free-text log lines are hard to search and easy to leak through. Write one JSON record per AI call with clearly separate fields:

log.info("ai_call",     kv("requestId", requestId),     kv("model", model),     kv("promptVersion", "support-reply-v4"),     kv("inputTokens", usage.inputTokens()),     kv("outputTokens", usage.outputTokens()),     kv("latencyMs", elapsed),     kv("promptMasked", masker.mask(prompt)),     kv("responseMasked", masker.mask(response)));

Now dashboards for cost and latency never need to touch the text fields at all. You can also keep the two kinds of data for different lengths of time: metadata for a year, masked content for a couple of weeks. Put the request ID into your logging framework's MDC so every line belonging to one call, including retries and tool calls, carries the same ID.

Streaming trips people up. Tokens arrive in tiny pieces, and a card number can be split across two chunks, which means masking each chunk on its own will miss it. Collect the full response in a buffer, mask it once the stream ends, and log that. If the stream dies halfway, run the partial buffer through the same masker.

Tool calls are the other trap. When the model calls one of your Java methods, the arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the whole exchange: order details, account balances, addresses. Treat them as part of the prompt and response. Log the tool name, duration and outcome by default, and log arguments only after masking.

Masking lowers the risk but never removes it, so surround it with some ordinary discipline:

Give content fields a short retention period. Old prompt archives are liabilities.

Limit who can read AI logs. Debugging a model doesn't mean someone needs to read customer messages.

Encrypt log storage and the pipeline that feeds it.

Log the hashed user ID so you can find and delete one person's records when they ask.

Allow verbose logging in development with fake data, and enforce strict settings in production through configuration, not through people remembering.

A masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none, because everyone assumes the logs are clean. Write tests for it:

@Test void masksEmailAndCardNumber() {     String raw = "Contact me at asha@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111";     String safe = new RegexPiiMasker().mask(raw);     assertFalse(safe.contains("asha@example.com"));     assertFalse(safe.contains("4111"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[EMAIL]"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[CARD]")); }

Build a small set of messy, realistic samples: numbers with odd spacing, mixed languages, addresses inside sentences, text pasted from spreadsheets. Run them in your CI pipeline, and add a new case every time a leak turns up. A scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net too.

A few I'd watch for. Logging raw text at debug level and assuming production never enables it; debug flags get switched on during incidents, so mask at every level. Masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results. Letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs. Leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, which bypasses your masker completely. And treating masking as finished once it ships, when every new prompt template can bring new kinds of data.

Every AI call writes a structured metadata record with a request ID

All prompt and response text goes through a single masker first

Streams are masked after assembly, and tool arguments are masked too

Content logging is sampled, short-lived and access-controlled

Tests cover the masker, with a regression case for every past leak

Client libraries aren't dumping raw payloads into the logs

Good logs turn an AI feature from a black box into something you can actually debug, price and improve. The same logs can also expose the people who trusted you with their details. The way through is fairly plain: record metadata for every call, push all content through one well-tested masker, use pseudonyms when you need to follow a conversation, handle streams and tools carefully, and keep retention short. Set that up before launch, not after the first incident, and you get visibility without regret.

#10131. Architecting Governed, Self-Evolving AI Agents on Google Cloud

As enterprise cloud platforms scale to serve millions of concurrent users, tightly coupled microservices introduce cascading failure modes that no static runbook or threshold alert can anticipate. During high-velocity events like a Black Friday flash sale, Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) face an unforgiving reality: diagnose noisy distributed telemetry in seconds, or suffer cascading outages costing millions of dollars per minute.

While generative AI copilots have accelerated code authoring and log summarization, AI agents struggle to reliably remediate live production outages. An on-call engineer battling connection pool starvation does not need an AI agent offering troubleshooting tips or unverified pull requests that might not fix the root cause; they need a governed, self-evolving AI system that can:

In this Google Cloud research reference architecture, codenamed Project Chrysalis, we demonstrate how three foundational research breakthroughs combine into a unified, production-grade architecture that can run on Gemini platform and the Agent Development Kit (ADK). Across simulated Black Friday cache-stampede outages, this governed architecture cut time-to-first-mitigation from 15 to 45 minutes down to 1.8 seconds, reduced HTTP 5xx error rates from 72.7% to 80.0% down to 0.0%, dropped P99 latency from 519.8 ms to 18.2 ms, and evaluated 400 counterfactual traffic policies in BigQuery in ~0.5 ms.

Crucially, this self-evolving architecture does not operate as an unconstrained "black box". To ensure the agent remains secure, reliable, aligned, and contained against rogue behavior, every autonomous action is cryptographically bounded by Google Cloud's defense-in-depth security stack: Model Armor to sanitize incoming telemetry against prompt injections and data leaks; Google Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) and Binary Authorization middleware to cryptographically sign synthesized patches and block unverified code from mounting; Open Policy Agent (OPA) Policy Controller to enforce strict SLA guardrails that prevent self-inflicted outages; and Dual-Custody Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) governance to require explicit SRE sign-off before any permanent changes are made to the agent hierarchy.

To see why static playbooks and advisory copilots fail under pressure, consider a classic distributed failure cascade:

Conventional AI agents are frozen at deployment with fixed system prompts and pre-registered tools. When a novel infrastructure bottleneck strikes, a self-evolving AI architecture extends those baseline capabilities by synthesizing situation-specific mitigation tools at runtime, scoring the telemetry impact of every intervention, and codifying verified guardrails for future incidents.

For true autonomous resilience, the agent itself must evolve based on empirical evidence of what worked and what failed:

Self-evolving cloud agents are an active area of applied research focused on resolving the SRE Trilemma (balancing exploration safety, structural adaptability, and multi-step credit assignment) by unifying three research pillars on Google Cloud:

1.Serverless Counterfactual Simulation (Dream-RSI):Challenge: Testing unvetted rate-limiting parameters in live production risks throttling legitimate revenue or re-triggering outages.Mechanism: Production request traces are exported to Google BigQuery, where the engine replays hundreds of candidate token-bucket configurations in sub-millisecond vectorized memory sweeps to identify Pareto-optimal policies offline.

2. Tri-Level Co-Evolution (APEX):Challenge: Single-layer prompt tuning provides fragile band-aids, while unconstrained code self-modification risks system instability.Mechanism: Agent evolution is separated into three governed timescales:

3. Step-Level Shapley Attribution (AgentEvolver):Challenge: During chaotic incidents, multiple interventions occur in sequence; coarse outcome rewards cannot isolate which step healed the service and which caused collateral damage.Mechanism: AgentEvolver computes marginal Shapley credit across each execution span using pre- and post-intervention telemetry deltas (P99 latency, HTTP 5xx rate, and database pool saturation), isolating beneficial patches from erroneous ones.

We implemented this architecture as an interactive application on Gemini platform. The diagram above illustrates the closed-loop workflow across the Production Target Service, Agent Development Kit (ADK) Multi-Agent Plane, Self-Evolution Engine, and Defense-in-Depth Governance Pipeline.

Each phase of the interactive demonstration showcases a distinct stage of the agent's self-evolution:

To deploy self-evolving agents safely in production, our architecture enforces an unbroken four-gate defense-in-depth chain of custody. Every synthesized patch, distilled memory, and topology update must clear four sequential verification boundaries:

Across automated evaluations of Black Friday cache-stampede workloads, the self-evolving architecture delivered decisive operational gains over both manual triage and static advisory copilots:

#10127. Waypoint-1.5: Higher-Fidelity Interactive Worlds for Everyday GPUs

Waypoint-1.5 is Overworld’s next real-time video world model, built to bring interactive generative worlds to the hardware people actually own.

The first release of Waypoint showed that real-time generative worlds were possible. It proved that interactive world models could be more than passive video demos, and that locally runnable systems could begin to close the gap between generating a world and actually stepping into one.

Waypoint-1.5 builds directly on that foundation. This release improves visual fidelity, expands the range of hardware that can run the model locally, and takes another step toward interactive world simulation without datacenter-scale compute.

On desktop hardware including RTX 3090 through 5090, Waypoint-1.5 can generate real-time environments at up to 720p and 60 FPS. This release also introduces a 360p tier designed to run smoothly across a much broader range of consumer hardware, including gaming laptops, and (soon) Apple Silicon Macs.

The biggest change in Waypoint-1.5 is accessibility.

With Waypoint-1, we proved the core experience. With Waypoint-1.5, we wanted to make that experience available on more machines without giving up real-time interactivity. That meant building two model tiers: a 720p model for higher-performance hardware, and a 360p model optimized for broader deployment.

We also scaled training dramatically. Waypoint-1.5 was trained on nearly 100x more data than Waypoint-1, which significantly improves the model’s ability to generate more coherent environments and more consistent motion over time.

Under the hood, Waypoint-1.5 also incorporates more efficient video modeling techniques to reduce redundant computation across frames. That matters because real-time world models are not judged only by how a single frame looks. They are judged by whether the world responds instantly, stays coherent as you move through it, and remains usable on local hardware.

A lot of recent progress in generative video and world models has focused on visual fidelity. Those results matter, but fidelity alone is not what makes an interactive world feel real.

What people remember is responsiveness. They remember whether the environment reacts to them, whether motion stays coherent, whether the world holds together as they explore it, and whether the whole experience feels immediate instead of delayed.

That is the gap we care about most: the difference between watching a generated scene and actually being inside one.

If world models only run on large GPU clusters, they remain impressive demos. If they run locally on consumer hardware, they become something much more useful: a foundation for interactive entertainment, creative tooling, simulation, and AI-native environments people can actually explore.

Waypoint-1.5 is designed around that idea: not just better videos, but more responsive and explorable worlds that remain accessible on consumer hardware.

The first is local execution through Overworld Biome. This release is designed to run across a wide range of hardware configurations, and the updated Biome runtime makes local setup much simpler. With the new installer flow, users can go from download to running the model locally in minutes.

The second is Overworld Stream, which lets you try Waypoint-1.5 instantly in the browser with no local setup required.

Whether you want immediate access or full local control, Waypoint-1.5 is built to support both.

Additionally, we provide World Engine, our flexible, easy to use, core inference library powering our official clients, along with nearly a dozen third party clients and libraries.

Waypoint started with a simple question: what would it take for generative worlds to become truly interactive?

Early generative systems showed that models could produce convincing images and videos. But building environments that people can explore, control, and interact with in real time is a different challenge entirely.

Waypoint-1.5 is another step in that direction, improving fidelity and expanding hardware accessibility while continuing to push real-time interactive generation onto local machines.

We think the future of world models will not be defined only by what they can render, but by whether people can actually inhabit and interact with them in real time.

Download Waypoint-1.5, run it locally with Biome, or jump in instantly on Overworld.stream.

And if you build something fun, strange, or unexpectedly immersive with it, we’d love to see it.

#10124. Meet HoloTab by HCompany. Your AI browser companion.

We built one of the most powerful computer-use AIs in the world. And made it directly accessible from your browser. On March 31st, we released Holo3, our most advanced computer-use model to date.

Building something powerful is one thing; making it accessible and easy to use is another. We’re doing both.

HoloTab is a Chrome extension that navigates the web just like a person would. It automates tasks across any website with zero setup or technical skills required. You describe what you want, and the agent handles it directly inside your browser, navigating interfaces, filling fields, and making decisions the same way you would. The vision models, the action planning, the interface understanding, all of it is running underneath, working for you, and all you ever see is the result.

Some tasks are quick and forgettable, but others are long and repetitive, the kind that reliably eat up your afternoon. You might find yourself cross-referencing competitor pricing across twenty different e-commerce tabs to update a master spreadsheet, or filtering through a dozen job boards and company career pages to find new listings, painstakingly porting the details into a tracking doc to manage your applications.

That's where routines come in. You start a recording, and HoloTab captures what you do in your tab in real time while you click or narrate along the way, demonstrating what you're doing and why. Your screen and your actions give HoloTab everything it needs, enriching the routine with enough context to actually understand the goal.

Once the recording stops, a routine is generated. From then on, you can re-run your routine or schedule it whenever you need to, and HoloTab will handle the rest on its own.

Computer-use AI is going to change how people work, research, and get things done, both in their professional and personal lives, and that shift is already closer than most people realize. But it shouldn't require a technical background to access, and the benefits shouldn't accrue only to teams with engineers who know how to wire these systems together.

HoloTab is free and ready for everyone to use today: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/holotab/hlaoiikljjgcjdhkakedfngifaopbcop
